Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 102, verses 1–8:

(p-6245) In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Takathur (Rivalry in Worldly Gain)

It is Meccan, and its verses number eight.

(p-6246) In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[1–8] ﴿The mutual rivalry in worldly gain diverts you﴾ ﴿until you visit the graves﴾ [al-Takathur: 2] ﴿No! You will come to know﴾ [al-Takathur: 3] ﴿Again, no! You will come to know﴾ [al-Takathur: 4] ﴿No! If only you knew with certainty of certainty﴾ [al-Takathur: 5] ﴿You will surely see the Hellfire﴾ [al-Takathur: 6] ﴿Again, you will surely see it with the eye of certainty﴾ [al-Takathur: 7] ﴿Then, on that Day, you will surely be questioned about the bliss﴾ [al-Takathur: 8]

﴿The mutual rivalry in worldly gain diverts you﴾ ﴿until you visit the graves﴾ [al-Takathur: 2]: That is, the boasting about abundance in wealth, children and the like occupied you, so one of you says, ﴿I have more wealth than you﴾ [al-Kahf: 34], and another says, "I have more children than you," and so on with what diverts from earnest effort and extinguishes the light of readiness, the purity of innate nature and intellect, and the lasting spiritual perfections. Boasting and vying over these perishing things, the abundance of wealth and children, and the nobility of fathers and grandfathers, carried you off to every path. ﴿Until you visit the graves﴾ [al-Takathur: 2]: that is, until you perished, died, and became among the people of the graves, having spent your lives in evil deeds, and you did not, throughout your lives, awaken to what is the cause of your happiness and salvation. "Visiting the graves" is an expression for death.

Al-Zamakhshari cited evidence for this. Al-Shihab said: In it is an indication of the certainty of resurrection, for the visitor must inevitably depart from what he visited. For this reason, some of the Bedouin, when they heard it, said: "They have been raised, by the Lord of the Ka'bah!" Ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: Whoever visits must return to either a garden or a fire. Some eloquent writers called the graveyard "the vestibule of the Hereafter." (p-6247)

"No!" is a rebuke against occupation with rivalry and the delusion that success lies in boasting, for success lies in supporting the truth and adorning oneself with virtues. ﴿You will come to know﴾ [al-Takathur: 3]: that is, the outcome of what you are upon in the Hereafter, the dire consequence of occupation with these swiftly passing desires, whose burden is great, because their consequences endure.

﴿Again, no! You will come to know﴾ [al-Takathur: 4]: a repetition for emphasis, and "again" indicates that the second is more forceful than the first. Or the first refers to death, and the second to resurrection.

﴿No! If only you knew with certainty of certainty﴾ [al-Takathur: 5]: that is, if you knew what lies before you of recompense with the knowledge of the certain matter, then what cannot be described of regret and grief over the passing of your precious lifetime in rivalry and in heedlessness of the truth would have occurred. "Certainty" here means "that which is certain," an attribute of an omitted noun, or an attribute of "knowledge," on the basis of the attribute being added to the qualified noun. The omission of the answer to "if" (law) is demanded by reason from the condition and what precedes it, so that it may be firmly established with exceptional firmness.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿You will surely see the Hellfire﴾ [al-Takathur: 6]: the answer to an implied oath, by which the threat is emphasized, the warning is intensified, and what they were warned of is clarified, in order to magnify it.

﴿Again, you will surely see it with the eye of certainty﴾ [al-Takathur: 7]: that is, the seeing which is itself certainty. Here "eye" means "self," as in "Zayd came, his eye," meaning himself. It was the very essence of certainty because unveiling through seeing and witnessing is above all other kinds of unveiling; so it is more deserving of being "the eye of certainty." The repetition is for emphasis.

The Imam said: Seeing the Hellfire is a metonym for experiencing its torment, and this is a common metonymy in the Noble Book.

﴿Then, on that Day, you will surely be questioned about the bliss﴾ [al-Takathur: 8]: that is, about the bliss with which the rivalry in abundance and the boasting in this world diverted you: what you did with it, from where you obtained it, upon what you spent it, and what you did with it. This includes what God bestowed upon them of hearing, sight, and bodily health.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Bliss" is the health of bodies, hearing, and sight. He said: God will question the servants about how they used them, though He knows better than they. This is His saying: ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — each of these will be questioned﴾ [al-Isra': 36]. Ibn Jarir said: In His report, exalted is He, He did not specify one kind of bliss over another, but generalized; so He will question them about all bliss. For this reason Mujahid said: that is, about everything of the pleasure of this world. Qatadah said: Indeed God, mighty and majestic, will question every servant about what He entrusted to him of His blessings and of His right.
